questions.problem:
Given that $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(xyz)$ and

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{yz}{\sqrt{1-(xyz)^{2}}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{xz}{\sqrt{1-(xyz)^{2}}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{xy}{\sqrt{1-(xyz)^{2}}},
$$

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ on which all partial derivatives of $f$ exist.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(xyz)$ is defined only when $-1\le xyz\le 1.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1\le xyz\le 1\}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function $\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{yz}{\sqrt{1-(xyz)^{2}}}$ is defined only when 

$$
\begin{aligned}1-(xyz)^{2} & >0 \\ (xyz)^{2} & <1 \\ |xyz| & <1,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives $-1<xyz<1.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\}.
$$

- Similarly, the domains of ${f}_{y}$ and ${f}_{z}$ are the same:

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivatives of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1\le xyz\le 1\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1<xyz<1\}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy),$ find the set of values $(x,y)$ on which $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ exists.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that $f(x,y)$ is defined when $xy>0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}.
$$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)) \\  & =x\cdot \frac{x}{xy} \\  & =\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

The function ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ is defined only for

$$
\begin{aligned}y\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the domain of ${f}_{y}$ is

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}=\{(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ exists on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}} & =\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}\cap \{(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y)\,:\,xy>0\}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy(z-1))?$

I. The partial derivative with respect to $z$ is defined at $(3,2,1)$

II. ${f}_{y}(1,1,2)$ is defined

III. ${f}_{x}(1,2,3)$ is defined
questions.worked_solution:
First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{xy(z-1)}\cdot y(z-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{xy(z-1)}\cdot x(z-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{1}{xy(z-1)}\cdot xy \\  & =\frac{1}{z-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.  

- Statement I is false. If we substitute $(3,2,1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(3,2,1)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(3\cdot 2\cdot (1-1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡(0),
$$

which is undefined.

- Statement II is true. If we substitute $(1,1,2)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,1,2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot 1\cdot (2-1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)=0,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(1,1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,1,2) & =\frac{1}{1}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. If we substitute $(1,2,3)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,2,3)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot 2\cdot (3-1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡(4),
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(1,2,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,2,3) & =\frac{1}{1}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II and III  only'.

questions.problem:
Given that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{x}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ and

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-\frac{x\operatorname{cos}⁡z}{y{sin}^{2}⁡z}
$$

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ where all partial derivatives of $f$ exist.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{x}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0$ and $z\ne n\pi $ where $n\in Z.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${f}_{x}(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0$ and $z\ne n\pi $ where $n\in Z.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

- Similarly, the domains of ${f}_{y}$ and ${f}_{z}$ are the same:

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,y\ne 0,z\ne n\pi \},\,n\in Z.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2)?$

I. Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(0,2)$

II. ${f}_{x}(1,0)$ is defined

III. ${f}_{y}(1,1)$ is defined
questions.worked_solution:
First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2) \\  & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2) \\  & =\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(0,2)$, where we have 

$$
f(0,2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({0}^{2}+{2}^{2}-2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡2,
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(0,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,2) & =\frac{2(0)}{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}-2}=0 \\ {f}_{y}(0,2) & =\frac{2(2)}{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}-2}=2\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(1,0)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,0)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{2}+{0}^{2}-2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(-1)
$$

which is undefined since $\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is defined only for $x>0.$ Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

- Statement III is also false. If we substitute $(1,1)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(1,0)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{2}+{1}^{2}-2)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(0)
$$

which is undefined since $\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is defined only for $x>0.$ Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".
